column2: Sadherujā, Shaktimati, Shakuni, Tridiva, Kramu, those born from the foot of Riksha, and another, Vegavahini,
Sipra, Payoshni, Nirvindhya, Tapi, the excellent river, Vena, Vaitarani, Sinivali, Kumudvati,
Toya, Mahagauri, Durga and Antahshila: these rivers born from the foot of Vindhya have holy waters and are auspicious.
Godavari, Bhimarathi, Krishnaveni, Apaga, Tungabhadra, Suprayoga and another, Papanashini,
issuing from the foot of Sahya: these are the best of rivers. Kritamala, Tamraparni, Pushyaja, Pratyalavati,
born of Mount Malaya, these are holy and have cool waters. Pitri, Somarishikulya, Vanjula and Tridiva,
Langulini and Vamshakara are remembered as born of Mahendra. Suvikala, Kumari, Manuga, Mandagamini,
Kshayapalasini are remembered as born of Shuktimat. All are holy Sarasvatis, all Gangas going to the sea,
all are mothers of the universe, all are remembered as removers of sin. Thousands of other small rivers have been mentioned, best of Brahmins,
some flowing in the rainy season, others always. The Matsyas, Mukutas, Kulyas, Kuntalas, Kashis, Kosalas,
Andhrakas, Kalingas, Shamakas along with the Vrikas: these countries are mostly called the Middle Country.
To the north of Sahya, where the river Godavari is, that region is delightful in all the earth.
The lovely city of Govardhana of the great-souled Bhargava; the Vahikas, Karatadhanas, Sutiras and Kalatoyadas;
the Aparantas and Shudras, Vahlikas, Keralas, Gandharas, Yavanas, Sindhu, Sauvira and Madraka;
Shatadruhas, Kalingas, Paradas, Harabhushikas, Matharas, Kanakas, Kaikeyas, Dambhamalikas;
countries near the Kshatriyas, families of Vaishyas and Shudras, Kambojas, best of Brahmins, Barbaras and Saulokikas,
Viras, Tusharas, men of Pahlavadhaya, Atreyas, Bharadvajas, Pushkalas, Dasherakas,
Lampakas, Shunashokas, Kulikas with the Jangalas, Aushadhyas, Chalachandra, and the tribes of the Kiratas,
Tomaras, Hamsamargas, Kashmiras, Karunas, Shulikas, Kuhakas and Magadhas:
these are the northern countries; now learn the eastern: Andhas, Vamankurakas, Vallakas, Makhantakas,
and the others: Angas, Vangas, Maladas, Malavartikas, Bhadratungas, Pratijayas, Bharyangas, Apamardakas,
Pragjyotishas, Madras, Videhas, Tamraliptakas, Mallas, Magadhakas and Nandas: the eastern countries.
Now the other countries, dwellers of the southern path: Purnas, Kevalas, Golangulas,
Rishikas, Mushikas, Kumaras, Ramathas, Shakas, Maharashtras, Mahishakas and Kalingas everywhere,
Abhiras with Vaishikyas, Atavyas, Saravas, Pulindas, Mauleyas, Vaidarbhas with Dandakas,
Paulikas, Maulikas, Ashmakas, Bhojavardhanas, Kaulikas, Kuntalas, Dambhakas, Nilakalakas:
these are the southern countries; learn the Aparanta: Shurparakas, Kalidhanas, Lolas along with Talakatas.
These are the Aparantas; now hear of the Vindhya dwellers: Malajas, Karkashas, Melakas with Cholakas,
Uttamarnas, Dasharnas, Bhojas with Kishkindhakas, Toshalas, Koshalas, Traipuras and Vaidishas,
Tumburas, Charas, Yavanas with Pavanas, Abhayas, Rundikeras, Charcharas, Hotradhartis:
all these peoples dwell in the Vindhya region. Next I shall tell of the countries that rest on mountains:
Niharas, Tushamargas, Kurus, Tunganas, Khasas, Karnaprāvaranas, Urna, Darghas, Sakuntakas,
Chitramargas, Malavas, Kiratas with Tomaras; the order of the four yugas, Krita, Treta and the rest, is established here.
Thus the Bharata varsha stands in nine divisions; its south, further side and east are the great ocean,
and the Himalaya lies to the north like the bowstring of a bow. This Bharata varsha, best of Brahmins, is the seed of all.
Brahma-hood, lordship over the immortals, god-hood, state of the Maruts, birth as deer, Yakshas and Apsarases, likewise serpents and reptiles,
and of all immovable beings, Brahmins, are measured by good and evil; the land of action is the means to reach them, and no other exists in the worlds.
Even the gods always have this wish: "Having fallen from godhood, may we obtain humanity on earth."
What a human does cannot be done by gods or Asuras, who are bound by the chains of that action and bent on exhausting it.
There is no varsha on earth equal to Bharata, Brahmins, where the varnas headed by Brahmins attain what they desire.
Blessed are the best of men who are born in the Bharata varsha; they obtain the great fruit of dharma, wealth, desire and liberation.
Where the fruit of austerity, supremely hard to get, is obtained, and the fruit of all gifts and all sacrifices,
the fruit of pilgrimage, the fruit of serving the teacher, the fruit of worshipping deities, the fruit of Vedic study, Brahmins —
where the gods are always glad to wish for a good birth, and the fruit of many vows, of many scriptures,
the fruit of non-violence and the like, rightly, the fruit of all desires, the fruit of celibacy and the fruit of the householder's life,
the fruit of forest life and of renunciation, the fruit of sacrifice and charity, and other such for those of good deeds,
is obtained in the Bharata varsha and not elsewhere, best of Brahmins. Who can tell all the virtues of Bharata, Brahmins?
Thus the excellent Bharata varsha has been rightly told by me: holy, removing all sin, blessed, increasing intelligence.
One who constantly hears or reads this with controlled senses is freed from all sins and goes to Vishnu's world.
with champaka, ashoka, bakula, karavira, patala, punnaga, karnikara, bakula, nagakesara,
tagara, dhava, bana, atimukta with kubjaka, jasmine and kunda flowers, and other flowers such as mallika,
with groves of ketaki bright with flowers of all seasons, kadamba, lakucha, sala, jackfruit, deodar,
saralas, mucukunda, sandal trees and others, ashvattha, saptaparna, mango and amrataka,
palms, areca fruits, coconut, kapittha, and many other trees, it is adorned on all sides.
There the holy field of the Sun lies, famed in the world, a full yojana all around, granting the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
There abides the god himself, the thousand-rayed day-maker, known as Konaditya, granting the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
In the month of Magha, in the bright fortnight, on the seventh, one with controlled senses, having fasted and come there, bathes in the sea,
purified in body and soul, remembering the day-maker god; having bathed in the sea by rule, composed at the night's end,
having satisfied gods, sages, humans and ancestors, Brahmins, coming out and putting on two washed, clean garments,
having sipped water, self-restrained, on the bank of that great ocean, sitting facing east at sunrise,
the wise one draws with red sandal-water an eight-petalled lotus, rich in filaments, round, with a raised pericarp;
he should put sesame, rice, water, red sandal, red flowers and darbha grass in a copper vessel.
If copper is lacking, best of sages, he should make a packet of aka leaves with sesame and the rest, cover it and place a vessel on the vessel.
Having performed the placement on the hands and limbs, with the limbs beginning with the heart, meditating on himself as the Sun, rightly and with faith,
the wise one should worship in the middle, in the fire-petal, in the south-west, in the wind-petal, in the north-east, and again in the middle.
Having worshipped the lotus — abundant, pure, essential, adorable, the supreme bliss — invoking the Sun from the sky there,
and establishing him on the pericarp, he should then show the mudra; having done the bathing and all else, meditating well composed on him —
the Sun on a white lotus, abiding in a disc of brilliance, tawny-eyed, two-armed, red, clad in garments red as lotus petals,
endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful, boon-giving, peaceful, adorned with a halo,
having seen the rising Sun like thick vermilion, he should take that vessel, kneel on the ground,
place the vessel on his head, with one-pointed mind and restrained speech, and offer the arghya to the Sun with a three-syllable mantra.
One not initiated gives the arghya by his name alone, with faith and feeling, since the Sun is to be attained by devotion.
In fire, south-west, wind, north-east, the middle and the east and other directions, he should worship the heart, head, crest, armour, eyes and weapon.
Having offered arghya, perfume, incense, lamp and food-offering, having chanted, praised, bowed and made the mudra, he should dismiss (the deity).
Those who offer arghya to the Sun with controlled senses, whether Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, women or disciplined Shudras,
always with devotion and a purified inner self, enjoy their desired objects and attain the supreme goal.
Humans who take refuge in the Sun, the god who lights the three worlds and moves in the sky, become vessels of happiness.
As long as arghya is not given to the Sun as prescribed, one should not worship Vishnu, Shankara or the lord of gods.
Therefore, resolutely, one should offer arghya to Aditya day by day, being pure, with flowers and lovely fragrances.
He who, well composed, gives arghya to Aditya on the seventh, pure and bathed, obtains the fruit he desires.
The sick is freed from disease, the wealth-seeker gains wealth, the learning-seeker obtains learning, the son-seeker has a son.
Whatever desire he contemplates as he offers arghya to the Sun, that fruit the wise man rightly obtains.
Having bathed in the sea, given arghya to the Sun and bowed, a man or woman obtains the fruit of all desires.
Then he should go to the Sun's temple, taking a flower, with restrained speech; entering, he should worship the Sun after circumambulating three times.
He should worship Konarka, best of sages, with supreme devotion, with perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense and food-offerings,
with prostrations like a staff, shouts of victory and hymns. Having thus worshipped that god, the thousand-rayed lord of the world,
the man obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices, freed from all sins, a youth with divine body.
Having lifted seven earlier and seven later generations, Brahmins, by a sun-coloured aerial car going where he wills, radiant,
sung to by Gandharvas, he goes to the Sun's world, and enjoys excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of beings.
When his merit is exhausted he comes here, into a foremost family of yogis, and becomes a four-Veda Brahmin, devoted to his duty, pure;
attaining Vivasvan's yoga he then attains liberation. In the month of Chaitra, in the bright fortnight, the Damanabhanjika pilgrimage —
the man who performs it there obtains the fruit told before; at the Sun's sleeping and awakening, at the sankranti, equinox, solstice,
on Sunday, on the proper tithi, or at parva time, Brahmins, those who make the pilgrimage there with faith and controlled senses
go to the Sun's world in a sun-coloured aerial car. There, on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, abides Mahadeva
famed as Rameshvara, who grants the fruit of all desires. Those who see that foe of Kama, after bathing properly in the great ocean,
with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, excellent food-offerings, prostrations, hymns, songs and charming instruments,
great-souled ones obtain the fruit of the Rajasuya and the horse-sacrifice, and supreme perfection.
In an aerial car going where they wish, garlanded with nets of little bells, sung to by Gandharvas, they go to Shiva's world.
Having enjoyed lovely pleasures till the called-for dissolution, they come here when merit is exhausted and become four-Veda men.
Taking to Shankara's yoga, they go then to liberation. The man who gives up his life in the Sun's field there
reaches the Sun's world and rejoices in heaven like a god; again obtaining human birth he becomes a righteous king;
attaining the Sun's yoga he then gains liberation. Thus, best of sages, the very rare field has been told by me,
Konarka on the ocean shore, granting the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
One who keeps the Sun in mind and circumambulates the sky has circumambulated all the gods.
The man who, taking one meal a day, worships the Sun on the sixth, observing restraint and vows, with devotion,
or on the seventh, fortunate ones, obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. One who worships the Sun with a fast day and night
on the seventh or sixth reaches the supreme goal. On the seventh of the dark fortnight, fasting, with senses controlled,
one who worships the Sun with offerings of all jewels goes to the Sun's world in a lotus-bright vehicle.
The man fasting on the seventh of the bright fortnight who worships the Sun with all white offerings
is freed from all sins and goes to the Sun's world. He should drink water spread in a packet of aka leaves,
in graduated increase to twenty-four, and then reduce one by one; with two years the observance would be complete.
This Arka-saptami, granting all desires, is praised, when on the bright seventh it falls on a Sunday.
That seventh is called Vijaya; what is given there has a great fruit. Bathing, giving, austerity, fire-offering and fasting —
all on the Vijaya-saptami destroy great sins. Those who perform shraddha when Sunday arrives
and worship Mahashveta obtain what they wish. Those whose righteous acts are always directed to the Sun
are not born in a family poor or sick; one who plasters with white, red or yellow clay
obtains the fruit he thinks of. One who, fasting, worships the Sun with varied, fragrant flowers
obtains the desires he wishes. One who lights a ghee lamp or sesame-oil lamp and worships Aditya does not lose his sight;
the man who gives lamps shines constantly with the lamp of knowledge. Sesame, purifiers, oil and the gift of a sesame-cow are the best;
in fire-rites and in lamps they destroy great sins. One who gives a lamp constantly in temples of deities, at crossroads and on streets
becomes handsome and fortunate. The first kind is with oblations, the second with juices of herbs;
one should never use fat, marrow, bone or resin. The lamp's course is upward, never downward;
and so the giver shines and does not attain an animal birth. One should never steal or extinguish a burning lamp;
the man who steals a lamp goes to bondage, loss, anger and darkness. The lamp-giver in heaven shines like a garland of lamps;
he who daily anoints (the image) with saffron, aloe and sandal gains in the next world wealth, fame and fortune.
A pure man, with red flowers mixed with red sandal, always offering arghya at sunrise, obtains success in a year.
From sunrise, turning around until sunset, standing, facing him, reciting some mantra or hymn —
this is the Aditya vow, destroyer of great sins. With arghya, with all the limbs, one should offer;
at sunrise, with faith, one is freed from all sins. The giver of arghya with a golden cow, a bull, land and garments
obtains a fruit that follows through seven births. Arghya should be diligently offered in fire, water, sky, on pure ground,
to an image or to a pinda. One should always offer facing him, neither with the right nor left slant;
or ghee and guggulu to the Sun with devotion; at that moment he is freed from all sins, no doubt. Shrivasa, a square (offering), and deodar,
camphor, aloe and incense, offered, take one to heaven. At the northern or the southern solstice,
having worshipped the Sun especially, one is freed from all sins; at equinoxes, eclipses and Shadashiti-mukha,
having worshipped especially, one is freed from all sins. Thus at all times, in all seasons, the man who
worships the Sun with devotion is honoured in the Sun's world. Having made an offering to the Sun with krisara, rice-pudding, cakes, fruit, roots, ghee and rice,
one obtains all desires. Having made libation with ghee, a man becomes successful in everything;
having made libation with milk, he is not joined with mental pain; having made libation with curd, a man obtains success in his work.
He who with concentration brings water for the Sun's bathing at holy places, pure and afflicted by austerity, reaches the supreme goal.
Having given an umbrella, banner, canopy, flag and fly-whisks to the Sun with faith, one obtains the desired goal.
Whatever substance a man offers to Aditya with devotion, Bhaskara multiplies it a hundred thousandfold.
Whatever evil done by mind, speech or body is all entirely removed by the Sun's grace.
The fruit obtained from worship of the Sun even for one day cannot be gained by hundreds of sacrifices with Brahmins and the prescribed fees.
The eleventh form of the Sun, named Varuna, abides in the waters; she nourishes creatures constantly.
The twelfth form of the Sun, named Mitra, abides for the benefit of the worlds on the bank of the Chandra river.
Living on wind, he practised austerity, standing with the eye of Mitra, always favouring devotees with boons of many kinds.
Thus this form for the world's good was ordained in the past; because Mitra stood there, therefore Mitra is remembered as supreme.
By these twelve forms, by that Savitri, the Supreme Self, this whole world is pervaded, best of Brahmins.
Therefore he is to be meditated on and bowed to in his twelve forms by devoted men, constantly, with the inner self absorbed in him.
